procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 17, 1967 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1210 of 1965, which maintained the appellant's conviction.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 1210 of 1965. They agreed with the trial court that the appellant was guilty of evading payment of customs duty by utilizing his official position. They considered the allegation of sending personal goods in postal vehicles as a 'technical' offense and did not examine the evidence related to it.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's order maintaining his conviction. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, cancelled the appellant's bail bond, and ordered the refund of any fine paid. The key issue was whether customs duty was leviable on goods sent from Goa to Bombay after Goa became part of India.

directions: His bail bond do stand cancelled.

issue.issue_text: Whether customs duty was legally leviable on goods transferred from Goa to other parts of India after its integration into India.

facts: Goa was liberated on December 20, 1961, and became a part of India. The 12th Amendment to the Constitution, effective from that date, formally integrated it as a Union Territory.
The goods in question were transferred from Goa to Bombay after March 27, 1962, at which time Goa was indisputably part of India.
The lower courts held that customs duty was leviable based on 'administrative instructions'.
A notification from 1950 had previously declared Goa a 'foreign territory' for the purposes of the Land Customs Act.
law: A tax or duty can only be levied or collected by the authority of law, not by administrative instructions.
Section 5 of the Indian Tariff Act, 1934, empowered the government to declare a territory *outside* India as a foreign territory for customs purposes.
This law did not empower the government to declare any part *of* India as a foreign territory.
application: The Court determined that once Goa became a part of India, it ceased to be a 'foreign territory'.
Consequently, the 1950 notification declaring it a foreign territory lost its legal effect, as the government was no longer competent to make such a declaration about a part of India.
The Court rejected the argument that duty could be imposed by 'administrative instructions', stating that this is legally impermissible as it lacks the authority of law.
The Court noted that the prosecution failed to present any statute or statutory rule that imposed customs duty on goods moving from the newly integrated Goa to other parts of India.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that no customs duty was legally leviable on goods transferred from Goa to other parts of India after its integration. This was because there was no valid law authorizing such a duty; the previous notification treating Goa as a foreign territory was no longer valid, and administrative instructions could not be used to impose a tax.

issue.issue_text: Whether a tax or duty can be levied or collected based on administrative instructions without the authority of law.

facts: An official was accused of evading customs duty by sending goods from Goa to Bombay after Goa had become a part of Indian territory (after December 20, 1961).
The prosecution argued that customs duty was payable on these goods.
The trial court and the High Court convicted the official, agreeing that customs duties were leviable.
law: The fundamental legal principle cited by the Supreme Court is that "No tax or duty can be levied or collected except by authority of law."
A notification from 1950, which had declared Goa a foreign territory for customs purposes, could not legally continue in effect after Goa became a part of India.
The government did not have the power to declare a part of India as a foreign territory for the purpose of levying customs duty.
application: The Supreme Court found that the prosecution failed to present any statute or statutory rule that imposed a customs duty on goods transferred from Goa to other parts of India after it became Indian territory.
The prosecution's only justification for the duty was the claim of a witness that it was based on "certain administrative instructions."
The Court explicitly rejected this justification, stating that administrative instructions are not a valid legal authority for levying a tax or duty.
It criticized the lower courts for incorrectly accepting that a duty could be imposed based on such instructions.
The Court reasoned that since Goa was part of India at the time the goods were sent, there was no legal basis to treat it as a foreign territory and impose customs duty.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that a tax or duty cannot be levied or collected based on mere administrative instructions. Any such levy must be explicitly authorized by a law passed by the legislature. Since the prosecution could not point to any valid law imposing the customs duty, the Court concluded that no duty was legally payable.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant had assets disproportionate to his known sources of income.

facts: The trial court had used the allegation that the appellant's assets were disproportionate to his known sources of income as a ground to support its conclusion of guilt.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the formal charges framed against the appellant did not include an accusation of having disproportionate assets.
The High Court, in its appeal judgment, did not examine this specific aspect of the case.
The prosecution did not argue or press this point during the hearing before the Supreme Court.
The Court also commented that, even if it were to consider the issue, the accusation appeared to be "without any solid basis."
reasoning.conclusion: Based on the facts that the issue was not part of the formal charges, was not considered by the High Court, and was not argued before it, the Supreme Court decided it was not necessary to go into that aspect of the case and therefore rejected it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant utilised his official position in sending his personal goods in vehicles engaged by the postal department.

facts: The appellant was accused of utilizing his official position to send his personal goods in vehicles that were engaged by the postal department.
This accusation was separate from the main charge of evading customs duty.
application: The High Court, which had previously heard the case, considered this specific accusation.
The High Court held that this particular offense, even if it were true, was of a "technical" and "trifling nature."
Because the High Court viewed the accusation as minor, it decided it was "unnecessary to examine the evidence" related to it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had rejected this issue by deeming it too trifling and technical to warrant an examination of the evidence. The Supreme Court did not examine the issue further, as it overturned the appellant's entire conviction on other, more fundamental legal grounds.

arguments.issue_text: Whether customs duty was legally leviable on goods transferred from Goa to other parts of India after its integration into India.
appellant_arguments: Goa had become a part of India under Article 1(3)(c) of the Constitution by the time the goods were transferred.
There was no statute or statutory rule imposing customs duty on goods transferred from Goa to other parts of India after its integration on December 20, 1961.
The goods in question were all sent after March 27, 1962, by which time Goa was constitutionally part of India.
respondent_arguments: The appellant sent various articles from Goa to Bombay without paying customs duty, implying that such duty was payable.
The High Court was influenced by the 'practical consideration' that there were considerable foreign goods in Goa that could be transmitted to other parts of India.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a tax or duty can be levied or collected based on administrative instructions without the authority of law.
appellant_arguments: No tax or duty can be levied or collected except by the authority of law.
The trial court and High Court wrongly held that customs duties were leviable based on mere administrative instructions.
The alleged administrative instructions were never produced in court, as privilege was claimed for them.
respondent_arguments: The trial court and High Court held that customs duties were leviable based on administrative instructions.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant had assets disproportionate to his known sources of income.
appellant_arguments: The accusation was without any solid basis.
The formal charges framed against the appellant made no reference to this accusation.
The High Court did not consider this aspect of the case, and it was not pressed in the Supreme Court.
respondent_arguments: The trial court supported its conviction on the ground that the appellant's assets were more than he could have acquired from his known sources of income.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant utilised his official position in sending his personal goods in vehicles engaged by the postal department.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contested the charge of misusing his official position to transport personal goods.
respondent_arguments: The appellant sent his personal articles in vehicles engaged by the postal department without paying any charge.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: No tax or duty can be levied or collected except by the authority of law; administrative instructions are not a valid legal basis for imposing such a levy. A territory that becomes part of India ceases to be a foreign territory, and any prior legal notification declaring it as such for customs purposes loses its legal effect upon integration.
obiter: Practical considerations, such as the presence of a large quantity of foreign goods in a newly integrated territory, cannot change the position in law.
It is not necessary to consider whether the government could have imposed a duty on goods from a newly integrated territory after its integration.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the entire basis for the conviction was legally flawed because no customs duty was lawfully leviable on goods sent from Goa to other parts of India after Goa's integration. Goa became a part of India on December 20, 1961, and ceased to be a foreign territory. The prosecution failed to produce any statute or statutory rule imposing such a duty. The lower courts erred in relying on alleged administrative instructions, as a tax or duty can only be levied by the authority of law, not by administrative fiat. Since no duty was payable, the charge of utilising an official position to evade customs duty must fail.
legal_tests_applied: No tax or duty can be levied or collected except by authority of law.

When a territory becomes a part of India, it ceases to be a foreign territory, and laws applicable to trade with foreign territories (like a notification under the Indian Tariff Act declaring it a foreign territory) cease to have legal effect.
policy_considerations: The court explicitly rejected the High Court's reliance on 'practical considerations', such as the likelihood that considerable foreign goods were in Goa and available for transmission to other parts of India, stating that such circumstances do not change the position in law.
